papers.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Cause-of-Death Assignment From Verbal Autopsy Records: A National Benchmark Study in South Africa
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Timely cause-of-death (COD) information guides health policy, yet many deaths in low- and middle-income countries are not medically certified. In Africa, fewer than 10% of deaths are. Verbal autopsy (VA) yields a structured symptom questionnaire and a free-text narrative. Mortality surveillance increasingly records the narrative alongside the questionnaire, but the algorithms used to produce VA-based statistics were designed for structured responses only, so narratives inform physician COD assignment but do not contribute to algorithmic COD assignment. We evaluated whether supervised models could use both modalities to improve COD assignment. METHODS We analyzed 4,999 VA records for deaths at ages 12 years or older from a national sample of registered deaths in South Africa (RSA), using physician-assigned CODs as the reference standard. We trained unimodal and multimodal pipelines on the labelled records: pretrained language models (PLMs) fine-tuned on narratives alone, machine learning (ML) models on structured responses alone, and the two combined at the data, feature, and decision levels. We also prompted a locally deployed generative large language model (LLM) on the same unimodal and multimodal inputs, without parameter updates. All were compared with InSilicoVA, the operational comparator representing current automated practice. We evaluated individual-level assignment, population-level agreement, calibration, and generalization across provinces in RSA, reporting these metrics rather than ranking pipelines on any one of them. RESULTS Every supervised pipeline improved on InSilicoVA by 8.5-15.9 percentage points in top-1 accuracy and 3.5-7.1 points in cause-specific mortality fraction (CSMF) accuracy. The narrative and structured pipelines performed similarly in aggregate but differed by cause: 63.9% of deaths received identical predictions, 11.6% were correct only from the narrative pipeline, and 13.6% only from the questionnaire pipeline, with the narrative pipeline more accurate for noncommunicable causes and the questionnaire pipeline for communicable causes. Against the unimodal approaches, the decision-fusion pipelines added 4.2-5.4 percentage points in top-1 accuracy, concentrated in the most common causes, whereas feature fusion with cross-modal attention improved the less common causes, adding 6.6 points (95% CI, 1.7-11.5) in balanced accuracy and 5.5 points (95% CI, 0.6-10.3) in macro F1. Feature fusion reached the highest CSMF accuracy (95.7%). Paired differences from the better unimodal representative ranged from -0.2 to +3.4 points, with all intervals including zero. The LLM exceeded InSilicoVA on individual-level metrics and reached the highest balanced accuracy of any pipeline (60.6%), while the supervised pipelines retained higher CSMF accuracy. Supervised pipelines had lower expected calibration error than InSilicoVA. Supervised gains held across all nine held-out provinces, including every top-1 comparison and nearly every macro F1 and CSMF comparison. CONCLUSIONS PLMs using narratives alone substantially improved on current best practice and matched ML pipelines using structured responses, while multiple multimodal strategies produced further gains in individual COD assignment. The zero-shot LLM showed particular strength on rare causes, whereas supervised pipelines better recovered the population cause distribution. These findings support incorporating narratives as a core input to automated VA systems and evaluating representative fusion strategies for the intended output. External validation across settings and age groups will support broader implementation.

papers.title: Burden and factors associated with hospitalization among patients with chronic Diseases at a tertiary Hospital in Wolaita Zone, South Ethiopia: A Cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Background Chronic diseases are the leading causes of illness, disability, and death worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries. Hospitalization is a critical outcome in chronic disease management, reflecting disease severity, treatment failure, and healthcare utilization. However, data on hospitalization burden and its associated factors among chronic disease patients in Ethiopia, are limited. This study aimed to determine the rate of hospitalization and its associated factors among patients with chronic diseases attending a tertiary hospital in Wolaita Zone, South Ethiopia. Methods A facility-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 321 patients with chronic diseases attending the chronic follow-up clinic at Wolaita Sodo University Comprehensive Specialized Hospital from November to December 2022. Consecutive recruitment was used, with unique medical record numbers tracked to prevent double recruitment. Data were collected through structured questionnaires and medical record review. Negative binomial regression was used to identify factors associated with hospitalization rate, with incidence rate ratios (IRR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Of the 321 participants, 66% reported at least one hospitalization while on treatment, with a mean of 1.70 {+/-} 1.81 hospitalizations per patient. Drug discontinuation was the most frequently documented reason for hospitalization (39.5%), followed by disease complications (22.3%) and infections (11.7%). Multimorbidity was prevalent, with the majority (59.8%) had 2-3 conditions, and a mean of 2.40 {+/-} 1.02 chronic diseases per patient. Male sex was associated with a higher hospitalization rate, while regular physical exercise was associated with a lower number of hospitalizations. Conclusion This study found a high burden of hospitalization among chronic disease patients, with drug discontinuation being the leading documented reason. Male sex and regular physical exercise were significantly associated highlighting the need for medication adherence support programs and structured exercise programs integrated into routine chronic disease care, as well as gender-sensitive interventions.

papers.title: From Evidence to Influence: Medias Role in Informing Urban Health Policies in Bangladesh and Nepal
papers.abstract: Background Urban inequities are often masked by the misleading notion of an urban advantage, despite persistent unequal access to quality healthcare services. Moreover, negative perceptions about the urban poor and slum-dwellers persist, despite their substantial role in driving and holding up the urban economy. It is thus essential to work with the media to bring visibility to these realities, raise public awareness, and inform more equitable health policies. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), evidence remains scarce on how health-related information from media outlets influences policy decisions. This study aimed to understand how journalists get information, engage with stakeholders in the health systems, and contribute to influencing urban health discourse in Bangladesh and Nepal. Methods We conducted a cross-country exploratory qualitative study comprising 30 key informant interviews from Bangladesh and Nepal, including 17 journalists, 10 health policymakers, and 3 public health advocates. Participants were purposively selected to ensure diversity across media types, gender, and professional roles. Interviews were conducted between September 2024 and March 2025. Data were transcribed, translated, and analyzed thematically using NVivo software. Cross-country comparative analysis was carried out to identify common themes and contextual differences. Findings Across both countries, participants relied on multiple and diverse information sources. Government data were often prioritized as a primary source of information, although they were shaped by political influences and accessibility constraints. Research evidence was valued but underutilized due to difficulties in interpreting scientific articles. Urban health issues received limited priority in health news reporting due to journalists constraints in covering multiple issues and financial constraints for in-depth coverage. Additional challenges included inadequate health and urban health-related training, limited fellowship opportunities for investigative reporting, and restricted access to data, while health policymakers and public health advocates frequently questioned the credibility and use of media-reported information. Media engagement in policymaking largely remained indirect and issue-focused or event-driven. However, consistent media coverage raised public awareness and generated public pressure and, at times, indirectly influenced health policy decisions such as immediate inspection after reporting on pesticides, installation of oxygen plants during the pandemic, dengue surveillance, and tobacco control measures and actions. Conclusion In Bangladesh and Nepal, news media play a significant but indirect role in shaping urban health policy decisions. Enhancing journalists capacity, improving access to credible information and data, and continuous engagement of stakeholders could strengthen evidence-informed urban health policymaking. Furthermore, establishing greater independence of journalists and government and community recognition of their responsible health reporting could help and motivate the media to contribute more meaningfully to public debate and policy reform processes.

papers.title: Risk Factors for Hypertension in the Western Highlands of Rural Guatemala
papers.abstract: Objectives Uncontrolled hypertension is the leading preventable cause of death and disability worldwide, with nearly two-thirds of affected individuals living in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Despite this disproportionate burden, epidemiological data necessary to combat the development of hypertension and its associated complications in LMICs remains scarce. The objective of this study was to assess risk factors for elevated blood pressure and hypertension diagnosis among adults living in a rural indigenous region of Guatemala. Methods A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using physician assessment data from 359 patients aged 18 years or older, who participated in a 2022 paired community health worker and physician hypertension study in San Lucas Toliman, Guatemala. Outcome variables were systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and diagnosed hypertension. Risk factors examined included age, sex, body-mass index (BMI), smoking status, alcohol use, antihypertensive use, language preference, and other clinical and behavioral characteristics. Multivariable linear regression models were used to assess factors associated with systolic and diastolic blood pressure, while multivariable logistic regression was used for assessing diagnosed hypertension. Results Higher systolic blood pressure was associated with increasing age, higher BMI, Spanish language preference, and low-intensity physical activity. Diastolic blood pressure was positively associated with increasing BMI, pre-existing diabetes, and Spanish language preference. There was a negative association with high-intensity physical activity. Hypertension diagnosis was associated with increasing age, higher BMI, and pre-existing diabetes. Conclusion This analysis confirms established hypertension risk factors in a rural indigenous population in Guatemala and identifies additional risk factors that may be relevant in this setting.

papers.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding Antimicrobial Resistance Among Users of an Indian Digital Healthcare Platform: A Cross-sectional Online Survey
papers.abstract: Background: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global health threat, and India's high antibiotic consumption makes public knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) a critical determinant of stewardship outcomes. Existing Indian KAP evidence is drawn from small, localised cohorts, leaving a gap in nationwide, digitally-sourced data. This study aimed to describe antibiotic-related knowledge, attitudes and self-reported practices among users of a digital healthcare platform in India, examine demographic and regional variation, and identify potential areas for future stewardship interventions. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among adult users of the Tata 1mg platform (December 2025-February 2026), with participants invited via an in-app banner. Knowledge and attitude were each scored on a 0-4 scale (4 items); practice was scored as a percentage of applicable items answered favourably, with scoring adjusted for branching logic based on antibiotic-access route. Of 10,726 respondents who started the survey, 4,883 completed it (45.5%). City of residence was mapped to one of six regions (India's five statutory Zonal Council zones plus a North-Eastern region) for 4,187 respondents. Associations with demographic characteristics were assessed using multivariable linear regression, and regional differences were assessed using one-way ANOVA. A parallel survey of 256 physicians was conducted to enable patient-provider comparison. Results: Mean scores were: knowledge 2.28 (SD 1.19), attitude 0.91 (SD 1.14), practice 44.9% (SD 33.4); attitude, not knowledge, was the weakest domain. Older age was associated with higher scores across all domains (practice: B=12.52, p<0.001 for age [≥]65 vs. 18-34); city tier was independently associated with lower knowledge and attitude (Tier 3 vs. Tier 1: p=0.010 and p<0.001, respectively). Regional differences were non-significant for knowledge and practice but significant for attitude (F=2.56, p=0.026, ^2=0.003), driven by lower scores in the North-Eastern region. In the parallel physician survey, 55.5% of respondents estimated that more than half of their patients self-medicated before consultation. Conclusion: In this platform-based sample, attitudes were the weakest domain, not knowledge, and 42.0% said their last antibiotic did not come on a doctor's recommendation. The findings may inform digital stewardship touchpoints, such as point-of-purchase guidance and prescription verification, in line with India's National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0. As a cross-sectional survey of platform users, it cannot establish the relative contributions of knowledge, beliefs and access pathways to antibiotic use.

papers.title: Quantifying optimal AWaRe antibiotic use patterns in hospitals with a new benchmarking tool applied to cross-sectional point prevalence survey data from 10 countries
papers.abstract: Background: Both over- and under-antibiotic use pose major global health challenges, yet there is no consensus on how to quantify deviations from optimal prescribing or set evidence-based targets. We developed a benchmarking tool for inpatient antibiotic use and evaluated its application in 10 countries. Methods: We developed decision-tree models to estimate expected empiric antibiotic use for 11 indications, based on the WHO AWaRe book for two age groups: 28 days to 12 years and >12 years. We parameterised the models using country-specific antimicrobial resistance estimates in the 10 countries and cross-sectional Global Point Prevalence Survey (Global-PPS) case-mix data from 2021 for 10 countries and from 2015-2022 in a subset of five countries. We then compared estimated expected antibiotic use with observed empiric use (from Global-PPS) in defined daily doses for adults and days of therapy for children, across indications and AWaRe categories. Findings: In 2021, among patients aged >12 years, in all countries but one, observed empiric Access antibiotic use, as a proportion of total antibiotic use, was lower than expected and empiric Watch antibiotic use was higher than expected. Similar patterns were observed in all countries but one in patients aged 28 days to 12 years. The magnitude of discrepancies between expected and observed Access and Watch antibiotic use varied across indications and countries. The median observed-to-expected ratios of usage across countries ranged from 0.3-0.8 for Access antibiotics, and 0.7-5.3 for Watch antibiotics in patients aged >12 years in 2021. Temporal trends from repeated surveys from 2015 to 2022 showed little change in observed-to-expected ratios for Access and Watch antibiotics. Interpretation: This benchmarking tool uses Global-PPS data to quantify differences between observed antibiotic use and WHO AWaRe recommendations. Our tool can be adaptable to local guidelines, provides policy-relevant estimates of expected antibiotic use to support monitoring, procurement planning, and targeted stewardship intervention.

papers.title: Uncovering Social Media Influencers' Health Posts: A Youth-Driven Mixed Method Study
papers.abstract: Social media influencers serve as a key source of health information for adolescents but often lack expertise, have commercial motives, and may spread misleading or harmful content. This study examines the health-related content shared by influencers, the prevalence of advertising, and how adolescents evaluate potential benefits and risks. Using a mixed-methods approach, we employed a quantitative descriptive method involving citizen science (Study 1) and a qualitative content analysis (Study 2). In Study 1, 336 adolescents from 16 Austrian schools documented and categorized 2,147 posts from 255 influencers. The most common topics included sports and fitness (50.5%), beauty ideals (29.6%), food and nutrition (27.6%), and cooking (19.1%). Although advertisements appeared in 41.5% of posts, adolescents rated 60.4% of them as beneficial and only 4.5% as harmful. The qualitative analysis of a subsample of the 90 most prominent posts showed that adolescents appreciated motivational aspects (e.g., healthy eating) but often overlooked problematic elements such as misleading claims, sexualized body ideals, and the linking of health messages to commercial products. Enhancing persuasion knowledge and critical thinking through education, along with stricter regulation of harmful products, is crucial to safeguarding youth online.

papers.title: CBD use characteristics associated with perceived effects and satisfaction among CBD product users in Japan: an exploratory analysis of a cross-sectional web-based survey
papers.abstract: Background. Cannabidiol (CBD) products are sold in many forms for many purposes, but it is largely unknown which characteristics of real-world use relate to how users evaluate their experience. Methods. We analyzed an anonymous web-based survey of 377 CBD product users in Japan. We evaluated perceived-effect (0-5) and satisfaction (0-6) scores using main regression models of use frequency adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Separate supplementary models examined estimated daily CBD amount and other-cannabinoid co-use, purposes of use, or specific CBD amount-reporting status. Results. Use frequency was positively associated with perceived effects (B = 0.148, 95% CI 0.091 to 0.205) and satisfaction (B = 0.113, 95% CI 0.049 to 0.177; both p < 0.001). Estimated daily amount showed no clear association with either outcome after adjustment, whereas participants who reported specific milligram information had higher scores on both (B = 0.543, p < 0.001 and B = 0.559, p = 0.002). Amount-reporting status was associated with product form (tincture 48.5% vs 30.8%; smoking or inhalation 58.5% vs 75.7%; both FDR-adjusted p = 0.009), whereas no statistically significant group differences were found for age, sex, body mass index, use frequency, or sleep timing. Purposes of use and sleep-timing indicators showed no clear associations with the outcomes. Conclusions. Subjective evaluation of CBD use was more consistently related to how often CBD was used and whether a specific milligram amount was reported than to how much was reportedly taken, and amount-reporting status was related to product form. Specific CBD amount-reporting status may be a useful complementary dimension for characterizing real-world CBD use.

papers.title: Linking environmental antimicrobial resistance to human acquisition: evidence, knowledge gaps and a mechanistic framework
papers.abstract: The contribution of environmental reservoirs to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) acquisition in humans remains poorly quantified, despite extensive evidence that resistant bacteria and resistance genes circulate through wastewater, surface waters, food and other environmental matrices. The central difficulty is no longer to demonstrate that these reservoirs are connected, but to quantify the direction and relative contribution of the pathways linking environmental AMR to human acquisition. Here, we synthesize the main processes that need to be represented at the interface between the environment and humans and propose a mechanistic framework for Escherichia coli producing extended spectrum beta lactamases (ESBL Ec), linking human, water and food compartments. The framework explicitly represents contamination of the environment by humans and multiple routes of human exposure to environmental reservoirs, including drinking water, recreational water exposure and food contamination mediated by irrigation. We apply the model to two contrasting illustrative settings, France and Madagascar, and use scenarios involving antibiotic use, environmental contamination and climate to explore how changes in specific drivers propagate across compartments. The simulations show responses that depend strongly on the compartment, while sensitivity analyses identify wastewater treatment efficiency and parameters describing transmission, exposure and environmental selection at specific interfaces as influential components of the system. The framework is used to explore how different transmission pathways and environmental drivers can shape AMR dynamics across interconnected human and environmental compartments. By comparing contrasting scenarios and identifying the parameters that most strongly influence model behaviour, we highlight both potential leverage points and critical gaps in current empirical knowledge. More broadly, this work illustrates how decomposing One Health AMR into tractable reservoir interfaces can help structure future data collection and progressively improve our ability to quantify transmission between reservoirs.

papers.title: Unnoticed high human infection incidence for West Nile virus and Usutu virus in the Netherlands: evidence from a longitudinal nationwide cohort, 2020-2023
authors: F. R. M. van der Klis
papers.abstract: Background Ecological surveillance indicates (regional) establishment of West Nile virus (WNV) and Usutu virus (USUV) in the Netherlands. However, the incidence of human infections remains unknown. Methods We identified WNV and USUV infections in the Netherlands in 2020-2023, using a longitudinal, nationwide population-based cohort, applying a two-tiered serology approach based on protein micro-array and virus neutralization. IgG data were used to estimate overall seroprevalence and infection incidence, and to study antibody longevity. Study set-up enabled tracking of the period of seroconversion and linking of self-reported travel history. The analyses took account of the survey design and weights were incorporated to match the Dutch population distribution following census data. Findings Among 4290 participants, we identified 113 probable WNV and/or USUV cases, including 55 seroconversions. Thirty-six cases were confirmed by antibody neutralization, of which 12 seroconverted. Six confirmed seroconverters were identified as autochthonous infections. The overall weighted seroprevalence was estimated at 0.54% (0.21-0.87%) for WNV and 0.25% (0.09-0.40%) for USUV. The weighted incidence for autochthonous WNV and USUV infection was estimated as respectively 0.06% (95% CI 0-0.12%) and 0.04% (95% CI 0-0.09%). Interpretation The estimated infection incidence and seroprevalence of WNV and USUV indicate a substantial underdiagnosis of clinical cases in the Netherlands in 2020-2023. These observations highlight the need for increased awareness among physicians to identify cases and the need for continued paired syndromic-laboratory surveillance for these viruses.

papers.title: A Growing Burden, a Persistent Gap: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome Education and Emergency Department Trends in Michigans Legal Cannabis Market
papers.abstract: Background: Since Michigan's legalization of recreational adult-use cannabis in December 2018, health care providers in the city of Kalamazoo, Michigan, have informally observed an increase in cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) presentations, although the extent of this increase has not been formally characterized locally. CHS is frequently underrecognized and misdiagnosed, often resulting in repeated emergency department (ED) visits and substantial diagnostic costs before a diagnosis is reached. Despite this clinical and financial burden, it is unclear whether consumers are adequately informed of this risk through point-of-sale or public health resources. Methods: A cross-sectional environmental scan was conducted to identify publicly available educational content about CHS on the websites of licensed cannabis retailers in Kalamazoo and relevant public health agencies. Provisioning centers and public health websites were screened using a structured coding rubric developed specifically for the environmental scan to assess the presence, depth, web page placement, and intended audience of CHS-related content. Additionally, the electronic medical records at a local teaching hospital in Kalamazoo were queried to identify ED visits with a primary diagnosis of CHS from January 1, 2010 to December 31, 2025. Results: Before the legalization of marijuana, the hospital recorded six ED encounters with the primary diagnosis of CHS between January 2010 and November 2018, and 274 ED encounters between December 2018 and December 2025 (mean age: 29 years; 157 females, 123 males). The incidence rate of CHS-related ED encounters was 57.2 times higher during the post-legalization period than during the pre-legalization period (95% CI, 26.0-157.3; exact Poisson rate-ratio test, p < 0.0001). Among the licensed Kalamazoo provisioning centers reviewed, only one mentioned CHS as a warning but did not describe symptoms or offer medical guidance. CHS content was not identified on the websites of the state or local health departments. Conclusion: Despite the growing clinical concern regarding CHS, consumer-facing educational resources remain scarce. Although this study cannot establish a causal relationship between the availability of CHS-related educational content and the observed increase in ED encounters following legalization, it identifies a substantial lack of CHS-specific warnings in the evaluated consumer-facing resources. Given the clinical and potential economic burden associated with delayed CHS recognition, we recommend that Michigans existing point-of-sale pamphlet requirement be amended to include CHS-specific warning language.

papers.title: Gendered patterns of reporting childhood abuse and quality of parental relationships across 21 nations: Descriptive findings from the Global Flourishing Study (GFS)
papers.abstract: Childhood experiences are important antecedents of adult flourishing, yet gender patterns in these experiences are under-studied in large global samples using a common survey instrument and population-based study design. From the Global Flourishing Study Wave 1 data (2022-2024), we analyzed responses from 203,430 adults (51% female, 49% male) in nationally representative samples from 21 nations on eight childhood-related items: experiencing physical or sexual abuse, feeling like an outsider in the family, feeling loved by ones mother or father, quality of relationship with ones mother or father, health growing up, and perceived family financial situation. Greater negative experiences were noted in more affluent nations (as measured by gross domestic product (GDP) per capita), with negative experiences generally reported more often among females than males, again especially in more affluent nations. Gender differences were more pronounced when it came to relationships with mothers compared to fathers. Perceptions regarding health and family finance while growing up did not show appreciable gender differences and had weaker correlations with other items.

papers.title: Hand-Washing Hygiene Knowledge, Attitude and Practice among University Students in the Post-COVID-19 Era: A Case of KCMC University, Moshi, Tanzania
papers.abstract: BackgroundHand hygiene is a key public health intervention for preventing infectious diseases, including respiratory and gastrointestinal infections. Although the COVID-19 pandemic improved awareness and compliance, sustained adherence remains a challenge, with evidence showing a decline in practice after outbreaks, particularly among young adults in high-contact settings such as universities. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of handwashing hygiene among university students at KCMC University, Moshi, Tanzania, in the post-COVID-19 era. MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted among 380 students at KCMC University. Data were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire, which captured information on socio-demographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding handwashing hygiene. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Associations between variables were assessed using logistic regression and multivariable analysis, and a p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. ResultsA total of 380 students participated in the study, with a mean age of 23.5 {+/-} 3.5 years. More than half 209 (55.0%) were aged 18-23 years, while 203 (53.4%) were female. Most participants had access to hand hygiene facilities 338 (88.9%). 338 (88.9%) participants had good knowledge of hand hygiene but attitudes were mostly negative 193 (50.8%), and practices were suboptimal, with 201 (52.9%) showing poor hand hygiene practices. Good hand hygiene knowledge was associated with access to hand hygiene facilities (AOR=2.84, 95% CI: 1.25- 6.42, p=0.012) and formal training on hand hygiene (AOR=3.48, 95% CI: 1.24-9.76, p=0.018). Positive attitudes were associated with being in the fourth year or above (AOR=2.12, 95% CI: 1.16-3.89, p=0.015). Good hand hygiene practices were associated with access to hand hygiene facilities (AOR=2.67, 95% CI: 1.18-6.01, p=0.018) and formal training on hand hygiene (AOR=2.98, 95% CI: 1.19-7.48, p=0.020). ConclusionAlthough knowledge and awareness of handwashing hygiene were generally high among university students, inconsistencies between knowledge and actual practices were observed in the post-COVID-19 era. Strengthening health education programs and ensuring continuous access to handwashing facilities may improve adherence to proper hand hygiene practices among university students.

papers.title: Prevalence and Multi-Domain Determinants of Elevated Blood Lead Levels Among Pregnant Women in Bangladesh: Evidence from the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundLead is a cumulative environmental toxicant for which no safe level of exposure has been identified, and pregnant women and their fetuses are particularly vulnerable because lead readily crosses the placenta and can be mobilised from maternal bone stores. Bangladesh conducted its first nationally representative blood lead testing among pregnant women through the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), but a detailed, multi-domain analysis of the determinants of elevated blood lead level (BLL) among this population has not yet been reported. MethodsWe conducted a secondary cross-sectional analysis of 1,928 pregnant women aged 15- 49 years with complete data from the womens dataset of Bangladesh MICS 2025. Elevated BLL was defined as [≥]5 g/dL. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to estimate unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for co-exposure to arsenic, cadmium and mercury and sociodemographic and socioeconomic covariates. Slope Index of Inequality (SII) as well as Relative Index of Inequality (RII) were used to quantify wealth-related inequality. Population attributable fractions (PAF) were estimated for three counterfactual scenarios, and adaptive least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used as a sensitivity analysis. ResultsElevated BLL was present among 6.2% of participants. In the adjusted model, a 2-fold rise in blood cadmium was associated with higher odds of elevated BLL (aOR: 1.54; 95% CI: 1.21-1.96), whereas a 2-fold rise in blood mercury (aOR: 0.63; 95% CI: 0.48-0.83), rural residence (aOR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.32-0.94), secondary education (aOR: 0.49; 95% CI: 0.28-0.85) and post-secondary education (aOR: 0.22; 95% CI: 0.11-0.46) were associated with lower odds. Belonging to progressively wealthier quintiles was associated with markedly higher odds, BLL rising to an aOR of 10.32 (95% CI: 4.41-24.15) for the richest versus poorest quintile. The RII was 8.59 (95% CI: 4.24-17.40) and the SII was 0.159 (95% CI: 0.101-0.218), indicating a substantial pro-rich gradient in elevated BLL. Counterfactual scenarios suggested that shifting the population to secondary-level education could reduce the prevalence of elevated BLL by 52.9% (95% CI: 20.6-72.0) and shifting to rural residence by 24.3% (95% CI: 1.4-41.9). Adaptive LASSO variable selection produced estimates consistent in direction and magnitude with the fully adjusted model. ConclusionIn this national sample, approximately one out of every 16 pregnant women had blood lead levels that met or exceeded the action threshold set by the World Health Organization, with this issue being particularly prevalent among wealthier, urban, and less-educated women, and was compounded by co-exposure to cadmium. In Bangladesh, the typical pattern observed for maternal and child health indicators does not align with the inverse relationship found between household wealth and lead exposure. This suggests that the sources of exposure are not merely indicators of material poverty. Antenatal blood lead screening, source investigation, and equity-informed lead-reduction strategies that specifically reach wealthier and urban households are warranted.

papers.title: FERMAT: An Autoregressive Clinical Foundation Model for Disease Risk and Clinical Event Prediction
papers.abstract: Clinical foundation models learn patterns in longitudinal health records that can be reused across prediction tasks. However, the relative strengths of representation-based and generation-based prediction across clinical tasks remain unclear. Using longitudinal electronic health records from 3.77 million patients at a single hospital, we developed FERMAT (Foundation model for Exploring Real-world Multimodal health data using Autoregressive Trajectory modeling), a 65-million-parameter clinical foundation model. We compared predictions from task-specific predictors trained on patient representations with those derived from generated clinical event sequences. Representation-based prediction performed better in the disease-risk comparisons. In detailed analyses of five-year chronic kidney disease, fatty liver, and diabetes risk in a test cohort of 10,000 patients, representation-based predictors exceeded generation-based estimates by 0.098-0.115 in observation-weighted AUROC and had lower probability error. Generation-based prediction, in turn, performed better in predicting diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures recorded on the same day, a task motivated by the frequent presence of multiple events with the same date in hospital EHRs. Using 50 generated trajectories per patient, it achieved a Recall@10 of 71.0%, compared with 55.7% for representation-based prediction, with a paired improvement of 15.31 percentage points (95% CI, 13.92-16.79; n = 1,862). These findings demonstrate task-dependent strengths of representation-based and generation-based applications within a single clinical foundation model, providing an empirical basis for exploring how the two approaches can be used individually or combined to address clinical prediction needs.

papers.title: Sex differences in depression and substance use disorder diagnoses and overdose risk in British Columbia
papers.abstract: BackgroundDepression is a risk factor for overdose and is more commonly diagnosed among females. However, sex-differences in the association between depression, in isolation and in combination with substance use disorder (SUD), and overdose have not been examined at the population level in British Columbia (BC). This study described sex-and-age differences in associations between documented history of depression and/or SUD diagnoses and risk of fatal (FOD) and non-fatal overdose (NFOD). MethodsThis study used linked administrative health data from the Provincial Health Services Authority Platform for Analytics and Data. The sample included BC residents aged 19-79 as of January 1st, 2015 (n=3,996,690). Exposures were classified as documented diagnosis history of 1) depression; 2) substance use disorder (SUD); 3) depression and SUD; and 4) neither condition, using physician billing and hospitalization records from 2010-2014. FOD (BC Coroners Service records) and NFOD (BC Emergency Health Services records) were ascertained from 2015 to 2024. Incidence rates per 10,000 person-years and unadjusted incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using Poisson regression, with neither diagnosis as reference, overall and stratified by sex and age. ResultsThere were 14,281 FOD (78.59% male) and 43,555 NFOD (69.45% male) cases. FOD incidence was higher among males overall; however, relative associations between diagnosis history and FOD risk were stronger among females. Depression diagnosis history was associated with a FOD IRR of 3.95 (CI: 3.56-4.38) among females and 2.46 (CI: 2.32-2.61) among males. IRRs for SUD and for depression and SUD were larger among females (108.07 [CI: 95.83-121.73] and 116.70 [CI: 106.51-127.96]) than males (26.69 [CI: 25.57-28.18] and 31.21 [CI: 29.81-32.67]). NFOD findings were similar but attenuated (depression IRR: 3.22 [CI: 3.08-3.38]) in females; 2.29 [CI: 2.21-2.37] in males). ConclusionA documented history of depression and/or SUD was more strongly associated with FOD and NFOD risk among females, despite higher incidence overall among males. Future research should consider the potential role of other sociodemographic factors in explaining sex differences in associations between diagnosis history and overdose risk.

papers.title: Association of childhood experiences with wellbeing and flourishing outcomes in Indian adults: Evidence from the India Sample of the Global Flourishing Study (GFS)
papers.abstract: Structured AbstractO_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSChildhood experiences contribute to health and wellbeing across the life course, yet research from low- and middle-income countries has largely focused on a few outcomes rather than broader patterns of adult wellbeing, behaviors, and social and financial circumstances. MethodsIn this cross-sectional analysis, we used a nationally representative sample of adults in India (N = 12,765; aged [≥]18 years) from the Global Flourishing Study (GFS) Wave 1 (2023) to examine associations between eight retrospectively reported childhood experience items, 45 adult outcomes, and two composite flourishing indices. Survey-weighted linear, logistic, and proportional-odds models adjusted for age, gender, education, and residential setting, with Bonferroni correction were used to assess associations and effect modification by gender. FindingsAlthough the breadth and strength of associations differed across childhood experiences, less favorable childhood experiences were generally associated with poorer wellbeing and flourishing, greater odds of adverse health outcomes, and reduced access to resources and safety in adult life. However, outcomes related to prosocial behaviors showed a different pattern: childhood abuse (physical or sexual) was associated with greater odds of volunteering (OR 1{middle dot}31, 95% confidence interval or CI [1{middle dot}13,1{middle dot}51]), feeling like an outsider in ones family with greater odds of donating (OR 1{middle dot}80, 95% CI [1{middle dot}52,2{middle dot}13]), volunteering (OR 1{middle dot}53, 95% CI [1{middle dot}28,1{middle dot}82]), and helping a stranger (OR 1{middle dot}49, 95% CI [1{middle dot}27,1{middle dot}74]). Associations were broadly similar between females and males, with little evidence of gender differences. InterpretationAssociations of childhood adversity with poorer health and increased prosocial behavior in adult life may reflect unmeasured social, cultural, or dispositional factors and heterogeneous life-course responses. Nevertheless, these findings support strengthening child-protection, financial assistance programs, and mental health services in India.

papers.title: Prevalence of suicidal ideation and its associated factors among school-going adolescents in northern Bangladesh: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Adolescent suicidal ideation is a critical public health issue, yet empirical evidence on its prevalence and associated factors among adolescents in northern Bangladesh remains limited. This study estimated the 12-month prevalence of suicidal ideation and examined its associated factors among school-going adolescents in Nilphamari District, Bangladesh. A cross-sectional survey was conducted between May and June 2026 among 365 adolescents aged 13-19 years across eight secondary schools and colleges. Self-administered questionnaires assessed suicidal ideation alongside validated tools for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and perceived social support (MSPSS). Factors associated with suicidal ideation were examined using multivariable logistic regression. The 12-month prevalence of suicidal ideation was 30.7% (112/365; 95% CI 26.0%-35.7%). In the primary multivariable model, moderate depression (AOR = 6.05, 95% CI 1.03-35.38; p = 0.046) and moderately severe depression (AOR = 6.86, 95% CI 1.05-44.62; p = 0.044) were associated with higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to minimal depression. However, this association was not statistically significant in a sensitivity analysis using the PHQ-8 score after excluding Item 9 (AOR = 1.06, 95% CI: 0.96-1.17; p = 0.228). Loneliness "often" showed the strongest association with suicidal ideation (AOR = 10.59, 95% CI: 2.53-44.35; p = 0.001). Suicidal ideation was also associated with truancy of 6-9 days (AOR 4.44, 95% CI 1.24-15.90; p = 0.022), truancy of [≥]10 days (AOR 3.77, 95% CI 1.34-10.59; p = 0.012), intentional self-harm (AOR = 2.51, 95% CI: 1.17-5.41; p = 0.018), and physical harm exposure (AOR = 2.63, 95% CI: 1.24-5.57; p = 0.012). Maternal secondary education was associated with lower odds of suicidal ideation (AOR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.12-0.99; p = 0.048). Suicidal ideation was common among school-going adolescents in northern Bangladesh, affecting nearly one in three participants. Early school-based identification and support for adolescents experiencing mental-health and psychosocial difficulties, together with family engagement and strengthened suicide-prevention services, are warranted.

papers.title: Laboratory Evaluation of Cyclospora cayetanensis in Wastewater: Expanding Pathogen Targets for Regulatory Public Health Surveillance
papers.abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has become a cornerstone of public health surveillance, yet routine regulatory monitoring remains largely focused on respiratory viruses and selecting antimicrobial resistant bacteria. Emerging foodborne parasites, such as Cyclospora cayetanensis, remain excluded from standard environmental surveillance panels despite increasing domestic outbreaks. This study presents a laboratory-based pilot protocol evaluating the feasibility of extracting and quantifying C. cayetanensis from urban wastewater across the Chicago metropolitan area. Using sample concentration via centrifugation and mechanical bead-beating, automated magnetic bead nucleic acid extraction, and digital PCR (dPCR), we demonstrate high-sensitivity detection in municipal influents and sewer nodes. These findings establish a proof-of-concept laboratory methodology to support the expansion of regulatory public health surveillance frameworks to include non-routine protozoan pathogens.

papers.title: Daylight Saving Time, Acute Sleep Disruption, and Return-to-Baseline Patterns in All of Us Fitbit Data
papers.abstract: Seasonal daylight saving time (DST) transitions abruptly alter the alignment between clock time, environmental light, and sleep. In preregistered analyses, we used longitudinal Fitbit data from the All of Us Research Program to compare sleep around 13 seasonal transitions in Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah with sleep on the same dates in Arizona, where clocks do not change. The sample included 1,522 participants and 6,658 participant-transition windows. Following the spring transition, sleep duration changed more from one night to the next in Mountain states than in Arizona (14.6 minutes, 95% CI [7.2, 22.0]), even though sleep duration itself on day +1 showed little evidence of a DST-related reduction (-8.4 minutes, 95% CI [-17.3, 0.6]). Sleep timing shifted later after the spring transition and about 28 minutes earlier after the fall transition. Among Mountain-state observations with a large post-transition departure from usual sleep duration, the median return to the usual range was two nights. Nearly the same two-night pattern appeared in Arizona after similarly large sleep departures, indicating that this return pattern was not specific to DST. Greater baseline sleep-duration variability predicted a greater likelihood of remaining outside the usual range at days +7 and +14. Seasonal clock changes produced acute sleep disruption, while the Arizona comparison shows that a rapid return to baseline should not be interpreted as the duration of recovery from DST itself. Statement of SignificanceSeasonal daylight saving time changes are often studied with before-and-after comparisons, which can mix clock-change effects with ordinary variation across the week. Using Arizona as a calendar-matched no-clock-change comparison, we found that the Mountain-versus-Arizona difference in sleep duration on spring day +1 was similar to that on day -1, while the change from the preceding observed night was larger in Mountain states. In a separate Mountain-state analysis, large post-transition departures usually returned to the pre-transition {+/-}30-minute window within two nights. The same return pattern appeared on the same spring and fall dates in Arizona as well. This distinction shows why acute exposure effects and threshold-defined return trajectories should be evaluated separately in wearable studies.

papers.title: Socioeconomic determinants of elevated blood lead among children aged 12-59 months in Bangladesh: a nationally representative survey
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Childhood lead exposure is a major environmental health hazard whose social patterning is well characterised in high-income countries but poorly described in low- and middle-income countries. The 2025 Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7) measured blood lead in children aged 12-59 months, providing the first nationally representative biomonitoring data. Using the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (CSDH) framework, we identified structural and intermediate determinants of elevated blood lead (>=5 ug/dL). Methods: Of 18,905 age-eligible children, 10,622 (56.2%) had a valid blood lead measurement and 9,717 had complete covariates for multivariable models. Prevalences were survey-weighted (stratified-cluster Taylor linearisation). Survey logistic regression (adjusted odds ratios, aOR) and modified Poisson regression with robust variance (adjusted prevalence ratios, aPR) evaluated 20 a priori covariates across six CSDH domains. Robustness was assessed using inverse-probability-of-selection weighting (IPW), multiple imputation (m=20), seven selection-bias scenarios and bootstrapping (B=500). Results: The survey-weighted prevalence of elevated blood lead was 38.5% (95% CI 37.2-39.9). Maternal education was protective (aOR 0.83 per level, 95% CI 0.79-0.88), as were improved wall material (0.82, 0.69-0.96) and ownership of agricultural land (0.77, 0.67-0.88), livestock (0.77, 0.67-0.88) and the dwelling (0.54, 0.43-0.69); household crowding increased risk (1.08, 1.01-1.15). Household wealth showed a reverse socioeconomic gradient: prevalence rose from 30.2% in the poorest quintile to 51.9% in the richest, and the fully adjusted association was positive (aOR 1.24 per quintile, 1.13-1.37), strengthening rather than attenuating after adjustment for material conditions. The wealth penalty was attenuated, but not eliminated, at higher levels of maternal education. Adjusted odds ranged from 0.42 in Rajshahi to 2.99 in Dhaka (reference: Barishal). The wealth gradient was robust to IPW (aOR 1.26), multiple imputation (aOR 1.25) and all seven selection-bias scenarios. Conclusions: Elevated blood lead among Bangladeshi children follows a reverse socioeconomic gradient: wealthier households are disproportionately exposed, while maternal education and agrarian assets are independently protective. Lead surveillance and risk communication should extend beyond poverty-targeted frameworks to address urban, consumer and dietary exposure pathways.

papers.title: Longitudinal Associations between the Built Environment, Biological Aging and Cognition
papers.abstract: Features of urbanicity have been linked to poor psychiatric health in adulthood, but little is known about their relationship with biological age and cognition earlier in life. Using the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), we tested associations between the built environment and epigenetic ages (EpiAgeAltum, EpiAgeHorvath, EpiAgePACE) (n=2,452), brain age (n=751), and cognition (n=12,199). Analyses were replicated in Generation R and triangulated in the Millennium Cohort Study. The built environment was not associated with epigenetic ages ({beta}Altum range = 0.013-0.015, p range = .466-.689; {beta}Horvath range = -0.011-0.023, p range = .182-.728; {beta}PACE range = -0.045-0.013, p range = .131-.524) or brain age ({beta} range = 0.022-0.028, p range = .337-.429). A negative association with cognition was observed in Generation R. We provide no consistent evidence that childhood built environment exposure relates to biological age and cognition in adolescence, suggesting these relationships may emerge in later life.

papers.title: Probabilistic forecasting of prefecture-level influenza in Japan accounting for surveillance data release histories
papers.abstract: BackgroundPublic-health use of influenza surveillance - situational awareness, planning for clinical surge, and issuing advisories or warnings - needs more than an accurate point estimate of next weeks count. What matters operationally is whether a rise is caught early, whether the direction of change is right, and whether an alert threshold is about to be crossed, all with honest uncertainty. For such use a forecast must also respect reporting delay, later data revision, and the calibration of its prediction intervals. Using Japans sentinel surveillance, we evaluated short-term probabilistic forecasts that respect the data release history, and we measured what adding other surveillance series contributes, focusing on the properties that matter for public-health decisions. MethodsThe target was the number of influenza reports per sentinel site in each of the 47 prefectures. For each forecast we predicted, as quantiles, the value 1-4 weeks after the most recent observed week. We compared three models: a ridge regression trained jointly across prefectures; a gradient-boosting quantile regression (GBQR) that learns from many surveillance series; and their equal-weight combination on the log scale. Six seasons were used to develop the models. The 2025/26 season was held out as a temporal evaluation period after the specification was fixed; because its epidemic profile had already been seen, it is not a fully independent prospective test. We scored forecasts with the weighted interval score (WIS) and checked prediction-interval coverage. For the Japanese target series we used the value first published for each week; some auxiliary series were taken as retrieved and therefore include later revisions. ResultsIn 2025/26, the combinations WIS relative to a persistence forecast was 0.841, 0.811, 0.794 and 0.818 at horizons of 1-4 observed weeks - that is, 16-21% lower than persistence. Coverage of the 80% prediction interval was 79.7%, 77.1%, 74.5% and 75.1%, and of the 95% interval 94.3%, 93.4%, 92.6% and 91.8%. Adding auxiliary series improved the GBQR over the development period. However, on the original scale the combinations edge over ridge regression was not statistically clear, and in some low-level rising phases the combination did worse than ridge. ConclusionsOver the period studied, models that share information across regions scored better than a persistence forecast. For public-health use, however, the operative questions are the real lead time once reporting delay is accounted for, whether rises from low levels and threshold exceedances are caught in time, and whether the upper prediction intervals are wide enough; on these, the present evidence is not yet sufficient. The 2025 change to the sentinel system also means that pre-change advisory and warning thresholds cannot be read mechanically. A prospective evaluation with strictly controlled data availability is needed before such forecasts are used to support advisories or planning.

papers.title: Does active travel behaviour moderate the association between the built environment and depression?
papers.abstract: BackgroundBuilt environment characteristics have been associated with depressive symptoms, whilst active travel behaviour is linked to improved mental health. However, it remains unclear whether active travel buffers associations between increased exposure to the built environment and worse mental health. MethodsIn this pre-registered study, participants were 10,310 mothers (mean age = 28.11, SD = 4.83) participating in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC). A latent built environment factor was measured at study enrolment, active travel behaviour at a 2-year follow-up, and depressive symptoms at a 4-year follow-up. Moderation was examined using adjusted linear regression models including an interaction term between the built environment factor and active travel behaviour. ResultsThe built environment factor was positively associated with depressive symptoms ({beta} = 0.023, p = .012). Active travel behaviour was not associated with depressive symptoms ({beta} = -0.002, p = .854) and did not moderate the association between the built environment factor and depressive symptoms ({beta} = -0.002, p = .865), after adjusting for covariates, including age, familial depressive history, socioeconomic risk factors, physical activity, baseline depressive symptoms and smoking. ConclusionContrary to expectations, active travel behaviour does not modify associations between the built environment and depressive symptoms. These findings provide no evidence that active travel mitigates mental health risks associated with the built environment in this population. What is already known on this topicO_LISome features of the built environment have been associated with poor mental health, and active travel has been linked to better psychological wellbeing. However, it is unclear whether active travel can reduce the mental health risks associated with more urbanised environments. C_LI What this study addsO_LIWe tested active travel as a potential modifier of the longitudinal association between the built environment and depressive symptoms. C_LIO_LIWe found no evidence that active travel buffered this association in a sample of mothers. C_LI How this study might affect research, practice or policyO_LIEngagement in active travel alone may be insufficient to offset mental health risks associated with the built environment, and future research should test whether these relationships differ across populations, travel purposes and levels of active travel. C_LI

papers.title: Impact of conditional mobile data credits on caregivers use of an early childhood digital health intervention: a nested cluster-randomized controlled trial in Andean Peru
papers.abstract: As internet and mobile phone access increases, digital health interventions are increasingly used to support remote and low-resource populations. In many settings, the health impact of digital interventions is constrained by limited or short-lived engagement. We tested if conditional mobile data credit incentives increase digital intervention engagement within a digital intervention trial. This nested cluster randomized controlled trial was conducted with caregivers of children 3-9 months at baseline. Of 72 neighborhood clusters from the treatment arm of the parent trial (evaluating a digital early childhood development intervention), 20 were randomly assigned to treatment and 52 as controls. Eligible participants had a phone provider through which mobile data credits could be most affordably administered. Treated participants received around 250 MB mobile data credits every two weeks, conditional upon using the digital intervention at least once in the same period. Credits were digitally administered via a third-party service. Digital intervention engagement (primary outcome) was monitored continuously until endline data collection approximately 2 years after assignment. Secondary outcomes included caregivers views, behaviors, and early childhood development. We used intent-to-treat analyses to assess all outcomes. This trial was registered as NCT05202106 at clinicaltrials.gov and was completed in 2025. Participants were recruited between September 2021 and March 2023 (N Treatment = 147; N Control = 333). Conditional mobile data credits extended engagement with the digital early childhood development intervention by 6.50 weeks on average (treatment mean = 26.19 weeks, control mean = 19.69; p=0.011). No significant impacts were identified on secondary outcomes. As such, mobile data credits may be a cost-effective way for increasing caregiver engagement with digital health intervention in low resource settings.

papers.title: The Long Road to Care: A Mixed Methods Analysis of Referral Delays for Pediatric Injury Patients in Northern Tanzania
papers.abstract: Every day, 1900 children die from an injury, with the majority in low-and middle-income countries. In Tanzania, reaching definitive care, or the appropriate final level of care for a childs injury, often requires referral to a higher level facility. This hierarchical system introduces challenges that may lead to delayed care and, for severely injured children, cause mortality. The aim was to identify patient, healthcare provider, and health system-level barriers to timely referral for pediatric injury patients at the first site of care in order to identify targets for an intervention to reduce time to definitive care. In this mixed-methods study, a pediatric injury registry was established at three health facilities spanning three health system levels in Northern Tanzania. Thirty family caregivers of pediatric injury patients participated in interviews, while healthcare providers participated in four focus group discussions. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research framed interview guides and thematic analysis of the qualitative data. Of 782 patients enrolled in the pediatric injury registry from Aug 2024-Aug 2025, 269 were referred. Most visited 1-4 facilities before reaching definitive care (range 1-6). The median time from injury to definitive care was 15.1 hours (IQR 1.8-33). Qualitative data collection with family caregivers and healthcare providers revealed barriers to explain the delays to care in the outer setting (such as non-standardized referral pathways), the inner setting (such as delays in the decision to refer), and individual characteristics (such as inadequate training in pediatric injury care). According to the World Health Organization standards, every child who needs referral should be sent within 2 hours of arrival. To improve the referral delays found in this study, a locally co-designed, multicomponent health systems intervention for healthcare providers at the first site of care must be developed that includes pediatric injury care training and standardized referral decision support. Key MessagesO_LIInjuries are important contributors to child morbidity and mortality globally, with low-and middle-income settings like Tanzania disproportionately affected. C_LIO_LIIn Tanzania there is a complex health system where pediatric injury patients present to primary health facilities first, and are referred up the health system until they reach the definitive care that they need. C_LIO_LIBarriers at the outer setting, inner setting, and individual level of the health system contribute to delays in reaching definitive care. C_LIO_LIIn order to combat these delays and improve child morbidity and mortality, a locally co-designed, multicomponent health systems intervention at the level of the first site of care must be developed that includes standardized referral decision processes. C_LI

papers.title: Physicians' Industrial Action: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis Assessing Impact in 11 Kenyan Neonatal Units
papers.abstract: BackgroundSkilled healthcare workers are essential for neonatal survival; however, the Kenyan public health system has historically faced strikes compounded by a human resource crisis. Evidence on how strikes affect neonatal care and mortality remains limited. This study evaluated changes in neonatal admissions, clinical care processes, and inpatient mortality associated with 56 days of disruption during the 2024 Kenyan physicians strike. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective interrupted time-series analysis of 12,184 admissions to 11 Kenyan neonatal units implementing with the NEST360 Alliance, recorded in the Neonatal Inpatient Dataset from December 2023 to August 2024. Weekly admissions and inpatient mortality were modeled over a 72-week window (27,638 admissions) using hospital-clustered generalized estimating equations with seasonal terms. Care processes, case fatality, and birthweight-specific mortality were compared across study periods. ResultsWeekly admissions fell from 413 to 189 during the strike (incidence rate ratio (IRR) 0.49, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.31-0.75), approximately 1,700 fewer admissions than expected, and returned to baseline afterward (IRR 1.00, CI 0.81-1.23). Newborns admitted during the strike were of lower birthweight, more often premature, and more often outborn. Admissions fell across all birth-location categories, most steeply among inborn neonates. No measurable change was detected in documented inpatient coverage of care measures, in crude mortality (12.5% to 14.9%; risk ratio (RR) 1.07, CI 0.85-1.33), or in trend-adjusted mortality (IRR 0.88, CI 0.53-1.45). Case fatality among neonates with recorded infection doubled, from 4.7% to 9.6% (RR 2.06, CI 1.18-3.58; adjusted p = 0.047). ConclusionsThe 2024 physicians strike was associated with severe disruption to neonatal service utilization, with admissions returning to baseline when the strike ended. Among newborns who continued to reach care, inpatient mortality did not change measurably, but case fatality among those with recorded infection doubled. This analysis was confined to inpatient data; hence, the outcomes of newborns who did not reach the hospitals were not captured. Both inpatient and population-level data are needed to assess the full impact of the strike. Mitigating harm during future labor disruptions requires interventions such as resilient care models, formalized task-shifting protocols, and minimum service coverage agreements. WHAT WAS KNOWN?O_LIThe public health care system in Kenya experiences recurrent healthcare worker strikes during which maternal and general health services utilization is disrupted C_LIO_LINeonates are among the most vulnerable populations in the Kenyan public health system. However, few publications have quantified the impact of healthcare provider strikes on neonatal outcomes and processes C_LI WHAT WAS DONE THAT IS NEW?O_LIData from 11 Kenyan neonatal units, comprising 12,184 admission records from December 2023 to August 2024, were analyzed to evaluate changes in neonatal admissions, case mix, care processes, and inpatient mortality associated with a 56-day national physicians strike C_LIO_LIBecause the strike had an exact-dated onset and conclusion, both the disruption and recovery were estimated using an interrupted time series design, with hospital-clustered generalized estimating equations applied across all 11 units C_LI WHAT WAS FOUND?O_LIWeekly admissions fell by approximately half during the strike, an estimated shortfall of around 1,700 admissions against seasonal expectations, and returned to seasonal baseline once the strike concluded C_LIO_LINewborns admitted during the strike period were of lower birthweight, more often premature, and more often outborn. Admissions fell across every birth-location category but most steeply among neonates born in the admitting hospital C_LIO_LIThere was no measurable change detected in documented coverage of seven screening and intervention measures, or in inpatient mortality overall or by birthweight band. Case fatality among neonates with infection as the primary discharge diagnosis doubled. C_LI WHAT NEXT?O_LIInpatient data do not capture the outcomes of newborns who failed to access hospitals. Community-level data are necessary to quantify the full impact of service disruption. C_LIO_LIAs industrial actions continue to be increasingly prevalent with frequent disruption of services, mitigation strategies should be put in place to protect vulnerable patients. C_LI

papers.title: Hand hygiene knowledge and practices among health care workers in Uganda: Evidence from Mukono and Kagadi districts
papers.abstract: BackgroundHand hygiene (HH) is one of the most effective measures to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and limit the transmission of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens in healthcare facilities (HCFs). Effective HH programs depend not only on the availability of essential resources but also on healthcare workers (HCWs) knowledge, attitudes, and adherence to recommended HH practices. Despite the critical role of these factors in improving infection prevention and control (IPC), evidence on HH knowledge and practices among HCWs remains limited. In Uganda, such evidence from lower-level district health facilities is particularly scarce. This study assessed HH knowledge and practices, along with associated factors, among HCWs at selected health facilities in the Mukono and Kagadi districts of Uganda. MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted among 586 HCWs at selected health facilities in the Mukono and Kagadi districts from May to June 2025. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered via KoboCollect, covering participants socio-demographic and professional characteristics, HH knowledge, self-reported HH practices, and facility-related factors. Descriptive statistics summarized the data, and modified Poisson regression with generalized estimating equations (GEE), accounting for clustering of HCWs within facilities, was used to estimate prevalence ratios for factors associated with HH knowledge and practices. ResultsOverall, 82.1% of HCWs had adequate HH knowledge, and 43.0% had good HH practice. Nearly all respondents correctly identified the recommended handwashing duration (98.8%), the minimum effective alcohol concentration for alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) (98.8%), proper HH as the most effective method for preventing HAIs (97.6%), and 89.9% correctly listed all five WHO Moments for HH. HCWs in Mukono were more likely to have adequate HH knowledge than those in Kagadi (aPR = 1.36; 95% CI: 1.15-1.60). HCWs with 6-10 years of experience had higher knowledge of HH than those with less than two years of experience (aPR=1.16, 95% CI: 1.02-1.33). Good HH practice was significantly more common among clinical officers (aPR=1.36, 95% CI: 1.06-1.75) and other cadres (aPR=1.65, 95% CI: 1.14-2.39) than nurses and nursing assistants. ConclusionHCWs demonstrated high HH knowledge but suboptimal HH practice, suggesting a gap between knowledge and self-reported practice. Interventions should move beyond knowledge dissemination to strengthen compliance through multimodal, cadre-specific strategies, particularly for nurses and nursing assistants.

papers.title: Developing a social vulnerability index from real-world electronic health records using natural language processing
papers.abstract: BackgroundSocial vulnerability is associated with adverse health outcomes, but existing social vulnerability indices often rely on cohort-based and self-reported data, potentially limiting their population-level applicability. Therefore, this study aimed to develop an SVI from routinely collected electronic health records (EHRs) using natural language processing (NLP) and examine its association with mortality and healthcare utilization. MethodEHR data from 193,629 individuals aged 35-102 from the Wellbeing Services County of Central Finland between years 2010 and 2023 were used in this study. A 6-item SVI (total score 0-6) was developed from free-text clinical notes using deep-learning-based NLP. SVI scores were calculated at baseline and annually for individuals. Associations between baseline SVI and all-cause mortality and healthcare utilization were assessed over 12-year follow-up using Cox and count models. ResultsThe mean baseline SVI among all participants was 0.35 (range 0-6). Women had higher SVI (0.39) than men (0.32, p<0.001). SVI increased with age. One unit increase in SVI was associated with a higher risk of mortality (Hazard Ratio (HR) 1.23; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) (1.21-1.24), a higher odds of using healthcare services (Odds Ratio (OR) = 1.20; 95% CI): 1.19-1.21) and a greater healthcare service use (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) = 1.07; 95% CI: 1.06-1.07). DiscussionAn index capturing multiple domains of social vulnerability can be derived from EHRs using NLP. Higher SVI was associated with increased mortality and healthcare utilization. These findings support the potential of EHR data for assessing social vulnerability and related health risks. HighlightsO_LISVI can be derived from free-text EHR data using NLP in an unselected population. C_LIO_LIHigher EHR-derived social vulnerability was associated with mortality and healthcare use. C_LIO_LIEHR data may help identify individuals needing targeted assessment or support C_LI

papers.title: Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting Among Herbal Practitioners: A Mixed-Methods Study of Reporting Practices, Associated Factors, and Pharmacovigilance System Barriers in the Greater Accra Region, Ghana
papers.abstract: BackgroundHerbal medicinal products are widely used in Ghana; however, adverse drug reaction (ADR) reporting associated with these products remains limited, posing challenges to pharmacovigilance and medicine safety surveillance. This study assessed trends in herbal medicine-related ADR reporting, determined the prevalence and factors associated with ADR reporting among herbal practitioners, and explored barriers to ADR reporting in Ghana. MethodsA mixed-methods study involving secondary pharmacovigilance data review, an analytic cross-sectional survey, and qualitative in-depth interviews was conducted. Secondary data on herbal medicine-related ADR reports submitted to the Ghana Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) between 2014 and 2024 were reviewed descriptively. The cross-sectional survey involved 271 herbal practitioners selected through multi-stage probability sampling across seven districts in the Greater Accra Region. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and logistic regression in IBM SPSS Statistics version 26. The qualitative component involved 15 purposively selected participants, and thematic analysis was conducted using MAXQDA 2020. ResultsA total of 117 herbal medicine-related ADR reports met the inclusion criteria and were analysed from the Ghana FDA pharmacovigilance database between 2014 and 2024. Among 271 surveyed herbal practitioners, 11.8% (95% CI: 8.0-15.6) reported submitting at least one ADR report during the preceding 12 months. In multivariable analysis, lack of ADR reporting forms or job aids (aOR = 0.11, 95% CI: 0.04-0.31) and lack of exposure to Ghana FDA ADR reporting guidelines (aOR = 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03-0.32) were independently associated with lower odds of ADR reporting. Qualitative findings identified causal uncertainty, inadequate training, weak reporting systems, commercial interests, and limited regulatory support as major barriers to reporting. ConclusionADR reporting associated with herbal medicinal products was limited within the national pharmacovigilance system and among surveyed herbal practitioners. System-level barriers, particularly limited access to reporting tools and FDA reporting guidance, were associated with lower reporting. Strengthening pharmacovigilance infrastructure, improving practitioner training, and increasing access to reporting tools may improve herbal medicine safety surveillance.
